transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. Thank you for seeing me. Well, I suppose... gosh, where do I even start? It’s a bit of a long story, really. I mean, I’m 66 now, I don't work anymore, so I try to keep myself busy, you know, stay out of the house and stay active. So I go to church every Sunday, and I joined this walking club a while back just to keep my joints moving and get some fresh air. 

But... well, the reason I made the appointment is because of what's been going on with the people there. It’s just... even on my better days, you know, when I actually have the energy to get dressed and go out and I'm feeling alright, I just absolutely cannot shake this feeling. It’s the people at the church, and the ladies in the walking club. I just know they’re watching me. I can feel their eyes on me when I walk into the fellowship hall, and I catch them looking, and then they quickly look away. 

And it’s not just that they're watching me, Doctor, it’s... it’s the messages. They’re putting these little messages about me right there in the Sunday church bulletin. Just these tiny, specific phrases or Bible verses that anyone else would read right past, but I know they picked them out specifically for me to see. And then at the walking club, it's in the things they say to each other. They’ll be chatting about the weather or their grandchildren, but they slip in these words, these little coded messages about my life right in front of me. It just makes me so incredibly uncomfortable, and I spend the whole week just turning it over and over in my head trying to figure out why they are doing this to me.
How long have you been noticing these feelings of being watched and finding these coded messages—has this been going on for weeks, months, or longer?

Well, let me think... it's been quite a while now. I remember because it started right around the time I was trying to get my garden ready for the winter last year. So that would make it... oh, about eleven months now. Yes, eleven months. And it's not just the messages in the bulletin or the ladies at the walking club talking in code. It's the voices, too. Sometimes I hear them when I'm just sitting in my living room trying to watch my programs, or when I'm trying to fall asleep. And it just makes it so hard to keep my thoughts straight, you know? I'll be trying to figure out what they mean by the verse they picked for the bulletin, and then the voices start, and my mind just gets all jumbled up. I used to be so organized, Dr. Smith, I really was. I kept a meticulous calendar, I never missed an appointment or a birthday, but now... for these past eleven months, it's just been a struggle to keep everything straight in my head with all of this going on around me. It's exhausting, it really is. I just want to be able to go to church and walk with the club without feeling like I'm the center of this... this whole production they've put together.

During these past eleven months, have you also gone through stretches of feeling extremely low, hopeless, or on the flip side, unusually elated or full of energy, that lasted for a couple of weeks or more?

Elated? Oh, heavens no. No, I haven't felt full of energy in... well, I can't even remember the last time I felt anything close to energetic. But the other thing you mentioned, feeling low and hopeless... yes. Yes, very much so. In fact, that actually started even before I began noticing the messages and the ladies at the walking club acting so strangely. 

If I really sit down and trace it back... it's been about a year and two months now that I've just been carrying around this terrible, deep sadness. It's like a heavy, wet wool blanket, Dr. Smith, just weighing me down every single day from the moment I wake up. And the guilt... oh, the guilt is just awful. I sit in my chair and I just feel so terribly guilty for not doing more, for not being the organized, active person I used to be, for not keeping up with my house the way I should. 

And I've just completely lost interest in things that used to bring me joy. I used to love baking, you know? I would make these wonderful peach pies for the church bake sales, everyone always asked for them. But for the last year and two months, the thought of even getting the flour out of the pantry just seems completely impossible. I just look at the kitchen and I don't care about it anymore. I don't care about much of anything. 

It's just strange, isn't it? Because that deep, dark feeling, that complete lack of interest and all that heavy guilt, it was already sitting there right on my chest for a few months before they ever started putting those coded messages in the Sunday bulletin. I know exactly when it started because my great-niece had a baby shower about fourteen months ago, and I just couldn't bring myself to care or even go, and I felt so incredibly guilty about missing it. And I've just been stuck in that same awful, sad rut ever since, just dragging myself through the days. So no, definitely no high energy, just this long, long stretch of feeling so incredibly low.

Have there been any stretches of at least two weeks during this past year when your mood actually felt better or normal, but you still noticed the ladies watching you, the coded messages, or heard the voices?

Well, let me think about that... yes, actually. Yes, there was a time. It was... gosh, maybe a few months back? I remember because the weather had just started to turn, and I had this... this brief window where that heavy, wet blanket feeling I told you about, it just seemed to lift a little bit. It wasn't that I was elated or anything, just... normal, I suppose. Just feeling like myself again for the first time in ages. 

I remember I was actually getting dressed in real clothes instead of just staying in my robe all day, and I was eating a bit better, too. I even made myself a proper breakfast—eggs and toast, not just cold cereal standing at the sink. And the guilt wasn't pressing down on me so hard. I felt like I could breathe a little easier. That lasted for, oh, several weeks, I'd say. A good stretch where my mood just wasn't so terribly weighed down.

But the strange thing, Doctor—and this is what really bothered me, this is what kept me up at night even when I wasn't feeling so sad—was that even though my mood was better, all those other things didn't stop. Not at all. I was still sitting in my living room, feeling halfway decent for a change, and I would hear my name being called right there in the empty house. Clear as day. And I still went to church during those weeks, thinking maybe it would be different, maybe I could just enjoy the service since I had the energy to get there. But no, the ladies were still watching me, and they were still putting those little hints about my life in the bulletin and talking in code at the walking club. 

It was so frustrating, Dr. Smith, because I thought, well, if I'm feeling better, if the sadness is gone, shouldn't all of this stop? Shouldn't I be able to just read the bulletin without finding a message meant only for me? But it didn't stop. Even when my mood was perfectly fine for those several weeks, the voices and the hints and the watching... it all just kept right on going. It really makes you wonder what on earth they are trying to accomplish, doesn't it? Because even when I was taking care of myself and eating right, they just wouldn't let up.

Do you have any medical conditions—such as thyroid problems, neurological issues, or head injuries—or are you taking any medications, drugs, or alcohol that could be related to when these symptoms started?

Medical conditions? Well, let me think about that. No, my thyroid has always been perfectly fine. My mother, rest her soul, she had a terrible time with her thyroid—she was always so cold, always wearing a sweater even in July, and she had to take that little pill every single morning. But no, the doctor checked mine just last year when I had my annual physical, right before all this started, and he said my numbers were just beautiful. And neurological issues? No, nothing like that. My memory is sharp as a tack, except when the voices get so loud I can't think straight, but that's not my brain failing, that's just... well, an interruption, you see. 

And I've certainly never had a head injury. I've always been very careful. I don't climb on step stools or ladders anymore, not since my neighbor, Mrs. Gable, fell trying to change a lightbulb in her kitchen and broke her hip. It was awful, she was in rehab for months, so I just wait for my nephew to come over if something needs reaching. So no bumps on the head for me. 

As for medications, I just take a little something for my blood pressure, a tiny white pill, half a dose really, just to keep things steady. I've been on it for, oh, maybe fifteen years now, so it certainly didn't cause any of this to start happening just eleven months ago. And drugs or alcohol? Oh, heavens no! I don't drink at all, never have. My father was a bit too fond of his evening scotch, and I just never cared for the smell of it. The most I'll have is a cup of chamomile tea before bed, maybe with a little honey if my throat is scratchy. So no, Dr. Smith, there's absolutely nothing like that going on. My body is healthy, it's just... it's just everything else that's falling apart around me.

Looking back over the entire 11 months that you've been noticing the watching, the coded messages, and the voices, would you say the heavy sadness and guilt were present for most of that time, or was that period of feeling better and normal actually a bigger chunk of those 11 months?

Oh, my goodness, definitely the sadness, Dr. Smith. If I really sit down and look back at the whole calendar... well, I have one of those big Thomas Kinkade calendars hanging by the refrigerator, you know the ones? With the lovely little stone cottages and the warm glowing light in the windows? I use it to mark down all my appointments and birthdays and such. And if I think about all those pages I've flipped over since this all began, I can tell you for an absolute fact that for most of this whole stretch, that terrible sadness and the guilt and just... having absolutely no interest in my baking or my house or anything else... it's all just been sitting right there in the background. 

That little window where I felt normal, where I made myself the proper eggs and toast, that was really just a drop in the bucket compared to the rest of it. Just a few short weeks out of all those long, long months. 

Because the truth is, even on the days when the ladies at church seem to be minding their own business, or when the voices in the empty house are a bit quieter—because sometimes they do quiet down, you know, sometimes they're just a murmur, almost like they're whispering in the very back bedroom and I can't quite make them out—but even then, when the hints and the suspicious things aren't quite so loud, that heavy, wet wool blanket of sadness is still right there draped over my shoulders. It just waits for me. I'll be sitting in my chair, and the house will be relatively peaceful, but I'll still feel so terribly guilty and hollow inside. So yes, the feeling low and hopeless is absolutely the biggest chunk of the time. It just never really packs up and leaves, even when everything else gives me a tiny bit of a break.

I'm sorry, Dr. Smith, did you just ask me something? I think I might have completely missed your question. You'll have to forgive me, I was so caught up in thinking about that Thomas Kinkade calendar and how many pages I've had to turn while feeling so dreadful. He really was the Painter of Light, wasn't he? My sister gets me one of his calendars every single Christmas because she knows how much I love those little stone cottages with the smoke curling out of the chimneys. It just looks so peaceful, the kind of place where nobody is watching you and there are no hidden messages in the Sunday bulletin. 

But listen to me, I'm just going on and on again, aren't I? Sometimes once I get started on how heavy everything feels, it's like a faucet I can't quite turn off. It's just that it's been so long since I've really been able to sit down and explain all of this to someone who actually listens. What was it you were asking me just now? I promise I'll try to focus, though my mind does tend to wander a bit when I'm trying to untangle all these months in my head.

No, nothing like that. My memory is sharp as a tack, except when the voices get so loud I can't think straight, but that's not my brain failing, that's just... well, an interruption, you see. 

And I've certainly never had a head injury. I've always been very careful. I don't climb on step stools or ladders anymore, not since my neighbor, Mrs. Gable, fell trying to change a lightbulb in her kitchen and broke her hip. It was awful, she was in rehab for months, so I just wait for my nephew to come over if something needs reaching. So no bumps on the head for me. 

As for medications, I just take a little something for my blood pressure, a tiny white pill, half a dose really, just to keep things steady. I've been on it for, oh, maybe fifteen years now, so it certainly didn't cause any of this to start happening just eleven months ago. And drugs or alcohol? Oh, heavens no! I don't drink at all, never have. My father was a bit too fond of his evening scotch, and I just never cared for the smell of it. The most I'll have is a cup of chamomile tea before bed, maybe with a little honey if my throat is scratchy. So no, Dr. Smith, there's absolutely nothing like that going on. My body is healthy, it's just... it's just everything else that's falling apart around me.

inference.note: Medical/substance causes excluded (normal thyroid, no head injury, no drug/alcohol use), ruling out F06.2. The report of psychotic symptoms (voices, delusions of reference) persisting during a several-week period of normalized mood supports psychotic symptoms occurring independently of mood episodes, favoring schizoaffective disorder (F25.1, depressive type) over a purely mood-related psychosis, though primary psychotic disorder (F20.0) remains possible given the prominent, sustained delusions and hallucinations.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive episode has been present for the majority or only a minority of the total time she has had psychotic symptoms (watching, coded messages, voices), which is key to distinguishing schizoaffective disorder from schizophrenia with mood symptoms.
doctor.question: Looking back over the entire 11 months that you've been noticing the watching, the coded messages, and the voices, would you say the heavy sadness and guilt were present for most of that time, or was that period of feeling better and normal actually a bigger chunk of those 11 months?

patient.answer:
Oh, my goodness, definitely the sadness, Dr. Smith. If I really sit down and look back at the whole calendar... well, I have one of those big Thomas Kinkade calendars hanging by the refrigerator, you know the ones? With the lovely little stone cottages and the warm glowing light in the windows? I use it to mark down all my appointments and birthdays and such. And if I think about all those pages I've flipped over since this all began, I can tell you for an absolute fact that for most of this whole stretch, that terrible sadness and the guilt and just... having absolutely no interest in my baking or my house or anything else... it's all just been sitting right there in the background. 

That little window where I felt normal, where I made myself the proper eggs and toast, that was really just a drop in the bucket compared to the rest of it. Just a few short weeks out of all those long, long months. 

Because the truth is, even on the days when the ladies at church seem to be minding their own business, or when the voices in the empty house are a bit quieter—because sometimes they do quiet down, you know, sometimes they're just a murmur, almost like they're whispering in the very back bedroom and I can't quite make them out—but even then, when the hints and the suspicious things aren't quite so loud, that heavy, wet wool blanket of sadness is still right there draped over my shoulders. It just waits for me. I'll be sitting in my chair, and the house will be relatively peaceful, but I'll still feel so terribly guilty and hollow inside. So yes, the feeling low and hopeless is absolutely the biggest chunk of the time. It just never really packs up and leaves, even when everything else gives me a tiny bit of a break.

inference.note: The persistence of psychotic symptoms (watching, coded messages, voices) during a several-week period of normal mood confirms that the psychosis is not confined to mood episodes, ruling out a psychotic depression (MDD with psychotic features). Since mood symptoms have nonetheless been present for the majority of the illness course (14 months of depression vs 11 months of psychosis, with mood symptoms dominating most of that time), schizoaffective disorder (F25.1) remains the leading diagnosis, with schizophrenia (F20.0) retained as a differential pending further clarification of the proportion of time mood symptoms are absent.

I'm sorry, Dr. Smith, did you just ask me something? I think I might have completely missed your question. You'll have to forgive me, I was so caught up in thinking about that Thomas Kinkade calendar and how many pages I've had to turn while feeling so dreadful. He really was the Painter of Light, wasn't he? My sister gets me one of his calendars every single Christmas because she knows how much I love those little stone cottages with the smoke curling out of the chimneys. It just looks so peaceful, the kind of place where nobody is watching you and there are no hidden messages in the Sunday bulletin. 

But listen to me, I'm just going on and on again, aren't I? Sometimes once I get started on how heavy everything feels, it's like a faucet I can't quite turn off. It's just that it's been so long since I've really been able to sit down and explain all of this to someone who actually listens. What was it you were asking me just now? I promise I'll try to focus, though my mind does tend to wander a bit when I'm trying to untangle all these months in my head.

inference.note: Psychotic symptoms (delusions of reference, auditory hallucinations) persisted for several weeks during a period when mood was normal, confirming they are not solely mood-congruent and satisfy the criterion of psychotic symptoms occurring without prominent mood symptoms for ≥2 weeks. However, mood symptoms (depression, guilt, anhedonia) have been present for the majority of the total illness duration, arguing against schizophrenia (F20.0) as the primary diagnosis and supporting schizoaffective disorder, depressive type, as the best fit.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports 11 months of persistent psychotic symptoms (persecutory delusions of being watched, delusions of reference regarding coded messages, and auditory hallucinations) occurring concurrently with a major depressive episode (14 months of depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt, and functional decline) for the majority of the illness duration. Critically, there was a distinct period of several weeks where mood symptoms fully remitted (patient felt 'normal,' resumed self-care and eating) while the psychotic symptoms (voices, delusions of surveillance/coded messages) persisted unabated, establishing that psychotic symptoms occur both with and without a mood episode. This pattern—concurrent mood and psychotic symptoms comprising the majority of the illness course, plus documented psychotic symptoms in the absence of mood symptoms for 2+ weeks—satisfies criteria for Schizoaffective Disorder, Depressive Type, rather than Major Depression with psychotic features (which would require psychotic symptoms only during mood episodes) or Schizophrenia (which would not require prominent mood symptoms comprising most of the illness duration). No substance use, medical/endocrine cause, or neurological injury was identified to account for symptoms.
